newsitem.title: USA: INSTANT VIEW - U.S. Aug durable goods fall 3.1 pct.
newsitem.headline: INSTANT VIEW - U.S. Aug durable goods fall 3.1 pct.

text.p: Following are comments from U.S. economists after the Commerce Department reported August durable goods fell 3.1 percent.
U.S. economists in a Reuters survey had expected a 0.1-percent decline in orders.

VINCENT MALANGA, LASALLE ECONOMICS, NEW YORK: "One might wonder if (Federal Reserve Board Chairman) Alan Greenspan had the number before we did." Malanga was referring to the central bank's decision earlier this week to keep short-term interest rates unchanged despite some signs of strength.
Speaking on Reuters Financial Television, Malanga added that the data were healthy for the economy and were consistent with current quarter growth of around 2.0 percent.

DAN SETO, SENIOR ECONOMIST, THE NIKKO SECURITIES CO INTERNATIONAL INC: "Transportation was especially soft this month ... ex-transportation, the estimate was down 1.6 percent, but you also did see softness in other areas. As far as the (Treasury) market is concerned, this can be taken as one sign that the economy may be moderating, but we discourage people from reading too much into one month's ... orders."

JOHN CANAVAN, TREASURY MARKET ANALYST, STONE & MCCARTHY RESEARCH ASSOCIATES INC: "All in all, it looked pretty weak, even the details. It didn't look strong and the (Treasury) market has obviously reacted that way. Coming on the heels of the Fed's decision to leave rates unchanged, it really just continues to add to the very positive tone in the market at the moment. I know that aircraft orders were down and we were looking for that to be the case after very strong aircraft orders last month.
"Those who want it to lend credence (to the Fed decision) will see it that way, but we have to see a lot more data."
IRWIN KELLNER, CHIEF ECONOMIST, CHASE REGIONAL BANK:

"Durable goods are a volatile figure. But it clearly shows that the economy is losing momentum, and that growth in the third quarter is going to come in only a fraction of what it was in the second quarter, and that the Federal Reserve was clearly right in refraining from raising interest rates the other day.
"It looks pretty widespread. Commercial aircraft, motor vehicles and parts were down, and this drop of 3.0 percent was clearly many times what was expected," he added.

Kellner continued: "If you take transportation, it was down 1.5 percent. So, it is pretty clear this was a weak figure even allowing for the volatility. That, in combination with lack of inflation in most parts of the economy, suggests that the Fed did the right thing."

MICHAEL STRAUSS, EXECUTIVE VICE PRESIDENT AND CHIEF ECONOMIST, YAMAICHI INTERNATIONAL (AMERICA) INC: "It reverses the upside surprise we had in the month of July. After being about 2.0 (percentage points) stronger than expected, it's now about 2.0 (percentage) points weaker."
Strauss went on: "The biggest areas of weakness are the auto and aircraft components. The aircraft component is not going to be an area that's sustainable.
"The durables have been so erratic for a while that it's hard to get too excited about one month. The pattern for durables has been very strong this year.

"(In August) over the past eight years, the numbers have ranged from down 5.0 or 6.0 percent to up about 13.0 percent. August is a highly volatile month for the seires, (and) the series itself is highly volatile."

TIM MCGEE, CHIEF ECONOMIST, TOKAI BANK LTD: "It shows that the signs of strength we were seeing in orders were a mirage. It confirms (Greenspan's) view that the economy is slowing down. So, it would therefore be a mistake to raise rates now because if the economy is slowing down, he may need to lower them some time next year."

MICHAEL ENGLUND, CHIEF ECONOMIST, MMS INTERNATIONAL: "Non- defense capital goods numbers are quite weak. Non-defense was down, too. So the concentration of the orders weakeness in the non-defense capital goods sector should help the bond market."

Englund added: "For the economy in general, it suggests further evidence that we may be seeing some slowing in economic activity through the end of the year ... The fact that we see fairly widespread declines in the orders and the shipments data and the concentration of weakness in the non-defense capital goods is a good sign for bonds."

CARY LEAHEY, SENIOR FINANCIAL MARKET ECONOMIST, LEHMAN GOVERNMENT SECURITIES: "If you take out transportation, it's still down only 1.6 percent, but you've shifted the trend ... way back so the market's treating it very favorably."

"This suggests you could get a number on (Gross Domestic Product) below or well below 2.0 percent, maybe close to 1.5 percent. So that, combined with the (rise in jobless) claims is all very favorable for the front end of the curve."
-- N.A. Treasury Desk, 212-859-1660
